name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,169

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Eleanor admits yen for a dangerous 4

indicators.note: to admit is to let something in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: Eleanor Bron, the English actress and writer
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: A woman called Eleanor confesses a longing for some reckless poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 refers to 4 across, VERSIFIER, so the definition is a dangerous poet. Lady Caroline Lamb called Byron 'mad, bad and dangerous to know'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was a Romantic poet, famously described by a lover as risky to know.

clue.text: He described an Exmoor romance as dark and something else besides

blocks.note: a synonym for dark
more is something extra, in addition

explanation.surface: An author painted his West Country love story as gloomy and much else besides.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exmoor romance is Lorna Doone, set on the moorland of Somerset and Devon; its author was R D Blackmore.
explanation.definitionFit: R D Blackmore wrote the 1869 novel Lorna Doone, a romantic tale set among outlaws on Exmoor.

clue.text: “… passion acts upon the human mind in a — compounded of the acuteness of sense and constitutional heat” (Tobias Smollett)

definitions.text: “… passion acts upon the human mind in a — compounded of the acuteness of sense and constitutional heat” (Tobias Smollett)

blocks.clueFragment: “… passion acts upon the human mind in a — compounded of the acuteness of sense and constitutional heat”
blocks.note: a sentence with a gap for a noun meaning a proportion between two quantities
the source names the eighteenth-century Scottish novelist whose prose is quoted

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the missing word completes Smollett's sentence, and 'compounded of' two things points to a proportion between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a proportional relation between two amounts, here sensory sharpness against bodily warmth.

clue.text: It’s blooming Weller at last, valet now getting replaced

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word just before it
things replaced are put back in a different place, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: the final letter of the surname
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sam Weller, the bloody valet, is finally being swapped out for someone new.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's valet in Dickens, so 'Weller' and 'valet' seem to belong together; 'blooming' looks like British mild swearing but is the definition, a flowering thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Navelwort, or pennywort, is a flowering plant with round fleshy leaves that grows on walls and rocks.

clue.text: He’ll produce villanelles initially, whenever that’s right, without signs of hesitation

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it
without here means outside, so the sounds stand outside, ahead of the rest

blocks.note: first letter of the verse form
er is the sound of someone hesitating, and two or more of them are ers
if can mean whenever, as in 'if it rains I stay in'
i.e., id est, means that is
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A poet will turn out villanelles whenever the moment suits, never hesitating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Villanelles' is used twice: whole in the definition and for its first letter in the wordplay. 'That's' gives the abbreviation i.e., and 'without' places the hesitation sounds outside the rest, on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: A villanelle is a strict nineteen-line poem, and anyone composing such poems is a maker of verses.

clue.text: Invite caller finally round to see “The Glass Menagerie” here

definitions.note: a place described by a phrase; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it
brought round means turned about, so the letters are spun into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone asks a visitor over to watch Tennessee Williams's play at their place.
explanation.walkthrough: The Glass Menagerie is a Tennessee Williams play about Laura's collection of glass animals; the clue takes it literally, as glass ornaments that would sit behind glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A vitrine is a glass-fronted display cabinet, exactly where a collection of glass animal figurines would be shown.

clue.text: Thrashes Copperfield’s friend, taking one’s time

indicators.note: to take something away removes it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: Tommy Traddles is David Copperfield's loyal school friend in Dickens
T is the abbreviation for time, and is the letter taken away

explanation.surface: Someone beats David Copperfield's pal while being in no hurry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking one's time' reads as an idiom for going slowly; here the friend's name loses T, time.
explanation.definitionFit: Raddle is a dialect verb meaning to beat or thrash, so the third-person form matches.

clue.text: To put a girdle round about the earth in quatrain or ballad

definitions.text: To put a girdle round about the earth

indicators.note: in tells the solver to look inside the following words for the answer

blocks.note: found running across the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Puck's boast of circling the globe, set down in a short verse form.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is Puck's line in A Midsummer Night's Dream, 'I'll put a girdle round about the earth', so it reads like a quotation rather than wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To inorb is an old poetic verb meaning to encircle or enclose within a sphere, as a girdle surrounds a globe.

clue.text: “Cameraman” is to go courting in lady’s department

indicators.note: in places one piece within another

blocks.note: taken as written
a lady's thing is hers, giving the possessive pronoun
to woo is to court someone
D, short for dept

explanation.surface: A photographer's helper is off wooing in the ladieswear section of a store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cameraman' is in quotes because it is a nickname: Christopher Isherwood wrote 'I am a camera' in Goodbye to Berlin. The courting goes inside the lady's department.
explanation.definitionFit: The author's narrator declares himself a recording device with its shutter open, so the novelist is a figurative photographer.

clue.text: Capek’s play set on a lake in the country

indicators.note: set on means placed beside, so one piece follows another

blocks.note: R.U.R. is Karel Capek's 1920 play that introduced the word robot
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A Czech playwright's drama is staged on a lake out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: R.U.R. stands for Rossum's Universal Robots.
explanation.definitionFit: Rural describes places away from towns, out among farmland and villages, as opposed to urban.

clue.text: Switched on, start to play “Taxman”

blocks.note: Act I is the opening part of a stage play
VAT, value added tax, plus a man, ED

explanation.surface: Someone turns on the stereo and puts on the Beatles song 'Taxman'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start to play' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it means the opening act of a play; 'Taxman' splits into a British sales tax and a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that has been switched on has been set going or made operative, which is what activated means.

clue.text: Article in alternative setting, like H P Lovecraft’s gods

indicators.note: a setting holds a jewel, so one piece is mounted inside another

blocks.note: the definite article
or is the word that introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A piece of writing in an unfamiliar setting, reminiscent of Lovecraft's monstrous deities.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovecraft wrote a story called 'The Other Gods', and his pantheon includes the Outer Gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovecraft's tale is titled The Other Gods, so his deities are described by that adjective.

clue.text: Scene of assassination of King followed by Oliver

indicators.note: followed by puts the second piece straight after the first

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
Noll is the old pet form of Oliver, as in Old Noll for Cromwell

explanation.surface: Where Martin Luther King was killed, with Oliver coming next in line.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the King assassination; the definition is the grassy knoll at Dallas linked to Kennedy's murder.
explanation.definitionFit: A knoll is a small hill, and the grassy one in Dealey Plaza is famously linked to the Kennedy shooting.

clue.text: How mean one little conservative’s counterpart is, according to Private Willis

definitions.note: a phrase asking 'how mean?'; the answer is an adjective meaning mean

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
L, short for little
the party opposite the Conservatives in Victorian politics
points to the Gilbert and Sullivan song in which the pairing is sung

explanation.surface: A song lyric about how stingy small Tories are compared with their rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Willis, the sentry in Gilbert and Sullivan's Iolanthe, sings that every child born is 'either a little Liberal, or else a little Conservative'.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiberal can mean ungenerous or stingy as well as narrow-minded, so it fits a description of meanness.

clue.text: Surpassed unfashionable 4, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling is a sound-alike

blocks.note: something out is no longer in fashion
4 across is a poet; John Donne the metaphysical poet

explanation.surface: A dated poet has been beaten by others, so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 refers to 4 across, VERSIFIER, so the cross-reference asks for a poet; John Donne's name is said like 'done'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outdone is to be beaten or exceeded by someone else, a synonym for surpassed.

clue.text: Triplets found in an inferno

blocks.note: surface reading: three babies discovered in a blazing fire
setter's reading: three-line stanzas used in Dante's Inferno

explanation.walkthrough: 'Triplets' suggests babies and 'inferno' a fire; the capital is hidden at the start of the sentence, but it is Dante's Inferno, written in interlocking three-line stanzas.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian verse form chains tercets rhyming aba bcb, the scheme Dante used for the Divine Comedy.

clue.text: In one of which Olivia found love

definitions.text: In one of which Olivia found love

blocks.clueFragment: In one of which Olivia found love
blocks.note: surface reading: some setting where a woman called Olivia met romance

blocks.clueFragment: In one of which Olivia found love
blocks.note: setter's reading: the girls' boarding establishment of Dorothy Strachey's novel Olivia, where the heroine falls for a teacher

explanation.walkthrough: Olivia (1949), by Dorothy Strachey, tells of an English girl at a French finishing establishment who falls in love with its headmistress; the plural fits 'one of which'.
explanation.definitionFit: These are places of education, and the novel's heroine experiences a passionate attachment at one.

clue.text: Such as Ban Zhao is to start to record what’s current in her dynasty

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter
in places one group of letters within another

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of the word
I is the physics symbol for electric current
Ban Zhao lived under the Han dynasty of China

explanation.surface: Ban Zhao must begin chronicling the events of her own imperial line.
explanation.walkthrough: Ban Zhao (c. 45–117 AD) completed the Book of Han after her brother's death; everything before 'in' goes inside the dynasty's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ban Zhao is the first known female Chinese chronicler of the past, an example of the profession.

clue.text: Home perhaps of Prince of Aragon, a fool or a stupid leader turning up to retain silver

definitions.text: Home perhaps of Prince of Aragon

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is kept
in a down clue, turning up makes the letters read from bottom to top
to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
taken as written
taken as written
opening letter of the word
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: The Prince of Aragon is a fool, or a dim leader, rising up to keep the silver casket.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice the Prince of Aragon foolishly picks the silver casket, so the surface is apt; Saragossa (Zaragoza) is the capital of Aragon.
explanation.definitionFit: Saragossa is the chief city of the Spanish region of Aragon, so plausibly that prince's residence.

clue.text: Mar true representation? It might

indicators.note: a representation shows something in a new form, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what might spoil an accurate account, answered by the clue itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a misprint is something that might mar a true representation, and the first two words rearrange to give it.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is a printing or writing error, which by distorting the text spoils an accurate record.

clue.text: Chap, Italian, with unknown number of novels originally included

definitions.note: the answer is a proper noun, an Italian novelist

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so the opening letter is kept
things included are taken in, so a group sits within the rest

blocks.note: a chap is a man
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown numbers
o' is a shortened form of of, as in o'clock
opening letter of the word
I is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: An Italian man who wrote an uncertain number of novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian' does double duty as definition and as I; Z, O and N go inside MAN plus I. Manzoni in fact wrote just one novel, I promessi sposi, which adds a joke to 'unknown number'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alessandro Manzoni was the nineteenth-century writer of The Betrothed, the most celebrated novel in Italian literature.

clue.text: One with a particular advantage over Meursault?

definitions.text: One with a particular advantage over Meursault?

blocks.clueFragment: One with a particular advantage over Meursault?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who beats a character, or prefers a Burgundy wine village

blocks.clueFragment: One with a particular advantage over Meursault?
blocks.note: setter's reading: Meursault is the protagonist of Camus's L'Étranger, known in English as The Outsider, so his opposite is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Meursault is also a white Burgundy, a false trail; in Camus's novel he is the stranger or outsider, and someone with privileged access is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone within an organisation has privileged knowledge or access, an edge over anyone kept outside it.

clue.text: Look into the case? Morse has no alternative

indicators.note: to have none of something means lacking it, so letters are dropped

blocks.note: Inspector Morse, Colin Dexter's Oxford detective
or introduces an alternative; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Investigating a crime, Morse finds there is no other option.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse is known by his rank, and the rank loses its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect is to examine closely, and looking into a case is what a detective does when investigating.

clue.text: What Hatter had on top of table, consuming seconds about start of hour

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter
about means around, so one piece surrounds another
the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
eating is consuming food
s is the abbreviation for seconds
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The Mad Hatter's table spread, with guests helping themselves to more as the hour begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like second helpings, which fits the tea party, but it is just S; EATINGS goes around H. 'On' means 'on' the table in the surface but only links here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mad Hatter's party in Alice is a perpetual tea, so his table was covered in cups, pots and plates.

clue.text: Fielding may be a bit deep for this man

definitions.text: Fielding may be a bit deep for this man

blocks.clueFragment: Fielding may be a bit deep for this man
blocks.note: surface reading: the novelist Henry Fielding may be too profound for some reader

blocks.clueFragment: Fielding may be a bit deep for this man
blocks.note: setter's reading: in cricket a fielder posted in a certain position may stand deep

explanation.walkthrough: Fielding looks like the novelist; it is cricket fielding. Third man is a fielding position behind the batsman on the off side, often played deep, and the answer with 'man' makes the position.
explanation.definitionFit: Third man is a cricket fielding position, and deep third man is its variant placed near the boundary.

clue.text: Dye used by Montgomery’s laid-back girl on part of hair

indicators.note: laid back means set going backwards, so the letters run the other way
only a part of the word is used, its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
names the author whose heroine is wanted, L M Montgomery
Anne of Green Gables, heroine of L M Montgomery's novels

explanation.surface: A hair colouring chosen by a relaxed young woman in one of Montgomery's books.
explanation.walkthrough: Montgomery is L M Montgomery, not the British field marshal; Anne Shirley famously dyes her red hair and it goes green.
explanation.definitionFit: Henna is a reddish-brown colouring made from the leaves of a shrub, used on hair and skin.

clue.text: Where generals might be having a term of imprisonment

blocks.note: of can mean having, as in a man of means
lag is British slang for a prison sentence, as in an old lag

explanation.surface: Senior officers caught and serving a stretch behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: An Oflag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for officers in the Second World War; a lag in British slang is a convict or a spell in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Captured senior military officers were held in these German camps, short for Offizierslager.

clue.text: “They regularly retire every year at proper intervals to — of the spleen” (Oliver Goldsmith)

definitions.text: “They regularly retire every year at proper intervals to — of the spleen” (Oliver Goldsmith)

blocks.clueFragment: “They regularly retire every year at proper intervals to — of the spleen”
blocks.note: a sentence with a gap for a two-word phrase meaning to be confined, as in childbirth
the source names the Anglo-Irish author whose satirical prose is quoted

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Goldsmith mocks fashionable ladies who take to their beds with low spirits as if for a confinement.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase once meant to be confined to bed for childbirth, mocked here as a regular bout of melancholy.

clue.text: Nine to one on “King of the Lapiths”

blocks.note: IX is nine in Roman numerals
I is one in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A betting tip: nine-to-one odds on a horse called King of the Lapiths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nine to one on' reads as racing odds, with the definition in quotes as a horse's name; the numbers are Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Ixion ruled the Lapiths of Thessaly and was bound to a fiery wheel by Zeus.

clue.text: Are insolent possibly, cracking up at these

indicators.note: possibly means as one possible arrangement, so the letters may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to be reworked
these two letters are the ones left over once the answer is formed

explanation.surface: Being cheeky perhaps, laughing helplessly at these quips.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: 'Are insolent' is a possible rearrangement of AT plus the answer, so remove AT from those letters and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: These are short jokes or witty remarks in a single sentence, the things audiences laugh out loud at.

clue.text: One who might depict Tristan almost mad with agitation?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
agitation stirs things up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: the name without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A playwright who might portray Tristan as nearly driven out of his mind with distress.
explanation.walkthrough: Tristan, lover of Isolde, does go mad in some versions of the legend, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A playwright represents characters such as Tristan on stage, portraying their stories in drama.

clue.text: A little assassin in Japan

indicators.note: a little of something is only part of it, so the answer is a stretch of the text

blocks.note: spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A small killer operating in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay: the answer sits across the last three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninja were covert agents in feudal Japan, trained in espionage, stealth and assassination.
